subLevels.german: Es war einmal eine böse Königin und ihre Stieftochter Schneewittchen.

hints.hint: Schneewittchen = Schnee + an old form of weiß (a colour) + the diminutive -chen.
Same opener as Es waren einmal drei Bären, just in the singular.
If Pfeffer ~ "pepper", then Stief- ~ ?
If Tropfen ~ "drop" and Nacht ~ "night", then Tochter ~ ?
Königin is the feminine form of König 👑.

subLevels.reveal: Welcome to our abbreviated retelling of the German folktale Snow White, which, as we'll see, underwent massive changes from the Brothers Grimm to Disney.

subLevels.german: „Spiegel, Spiegel an der Wand, wer ist die Schönste im ganzen Land?“

hints.hint: You may be tempted to produce the rhyming Disney version, but translate the last phrase a little more literally.
Spiegel = a reflective surface. Wand is the surface where it's mounted.
die Schönste is the superlative of schön (beautiful). Use the canonical English word for this famous sentence.
You may have been tempted to translate "of them all", but we're asking for something a bit closer to the German.

subLevels.reveal: Der Spiegel, "The Mirror", is one of Germany's most influential news magazines (founded 1947). The Brothers Grimm actually wrote the line with the diminutive form Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand (using -lein, another diminutive suffix).

hints.hint: tausend + mal, the first part is a numeral
This time we're looking for a two-word translation of schöner, the comparative.
With Ihr, the mirror is addressing the queen very formally, but the formality will be lost in translation.

subLevels.reveal: Ouch! This mirror does not pull its punches.

subLevels.english: Who is the fairest in the whole land?
subLevels.explanation: For wh-questions ("who", "where", "what", etc), we're back to the same word order as main clauses, except that the wh-word must go in slot 1.
subLevels.reveal: We call them wh-words in English because all of them with the exception of "how" start with "wh". Happily, all the German equivalents start with w-: wer, was, wo.... Of course, this isn't an accident! They're all descendants of the same proto-Germanic words.

subLevels.german: Die Königin wollte Schneewittchen tot sehen, aber der Jäger konnte das schöne Kind nicht töten.

hints.hint: wollen ~ "will" in English, descending from a proto-Germanic word indicating "to desire", or "to w___".
Jäger we saw in the last level, what die Katze is to die Maus.
konnte is the past tense of können ~ "can".
töten = to make someone tot.

subLevels.reveal: The German literally says "The queen wanted to see Snow White dead", but its meaning is "wanted her dead", as we translated. tot and "dead" are cognates. It would have gone better for the queen if she'd insisted on witnessing the deed for herself.

subLevels.german: Die Königin wollte wissen, wer jetzt die Schönste im Land war.

hints.hint: We saw this verb earlier in Die Königin wollte Schneewittchen tot sehen, except that the hunter couldn't do the dastardly deed.
wissen is related to "wisdom". Think of a very similar noun, then take its verb form.

subLevels.reveal: Compare this subordinate clause with the same question in the main clause Wer ist die Schönste im ganzen Land? Notice any differences in the word order? The verb war "was" is now at the end of the subordinate clause! We'll wissen why very soon. By the way, wissen, "wit" and "wisdom" all trace back to the same proto-Indo-European root.

subLevels.english: The queen wanted to know where the hunter was.
subLevels.explanation: In main clauses, slot 1 is fairly free: it can take almost any word besides the tensed verb. In subordinate clauses, slot 1 is reserved for stand-in words — when the subordinate clause is a question, the stand-in words are wh-words like "who" and "what", standing in for the thing being asked about. Additionally, slot 2 is occupied by a subordinator like dass (English "that"), but when slot 1 is filled, it isn't said aloud.
subLevels.reveal: With the V2 slot filled by the silent dass, there is nowhere for the verb to move to, so it stays at the end of the subordinate clause. This explains the difference in verb position between main clauses and subordinate clauses. (Still skeptical? The next paragraph is for you! If not, skip to the final paragraph!) Okay, I admit this explanation may feel rather arbitrary. What's with this mysterious invisible, inaudible subordinator? If it weren't there, the verb could have happily moved to its usual second position just like in main clauses. But we have actual evidence that dass IS there from a dialect of German, Bavarian, where you can say things like "The queen wanted to know who THAT the fairest in the land was", i.e. the dass is said out loud! Now that we've simplified the noun phrase to just two words ("the hunter"), it's clear that English actually mostly behaves similarly: the most natural (pedants would say the only) translation of this sentence also leaves the verb at the end. This can be overridden by other preferences in English, but German is pretty strict. Verbs at the end of subordinate clauses, please!

subLevels.german: Die Königin wusste, dass der Spiegel die Wahrheit sprach. Schneewittchen lebte!

hints.hint: wusste is the past tense of wissen.
Wahrheit und Schönheit = ____ and Beauty. We'll see more of this suffix shortly!

subLevels.reveal: Another type of subordinate clause, this time with an explicit dass "that". It blocks the verb sprach from moving to the V2 position. Let's practise!

subLevels.english: The queen knew that the mirror spoke the truth.
subLevels.explanation: This time dass explicitly occupies the V2 position, blocking the verb from moving. There is no stand-in word to move to the first slot in the subordinate clause, so it cannot be filled.
subLevels.reveal: Ultimately, whether the subordinate clause starts with a stand-in word (accompanied by a silent subordinator) or an explicit subordinator (typically dass but also weil "because", wenn "if/when", ob "whether"), the rule is the same: the verb stays at the end. You can either have a subordinator, or a V2 verb. Not both.

subLevels.german: Die Königin gab Schneewittchen einen vergifteten Apfel.

hints.hint: Gift = 🧪☠️

subLevels.reveal: A classic German learner mistake is to say Ich habe ein Gift für dich; you're not offering a present, but poison. While they are cognates, German transformed the original sense of "something given" → "the dose given" → "the fatal dose" → "poison"; English kept the general sense. This is probably the most famous "false friend" pair between the languages. We've already seen the actual word for "present" in German, as brought by Der Weihnachtsmann — Geschenke.

subLevels.german: Der Prinz küsste Schneewittchen und sie wachte auf.

hints.hint: wachte auf is something that Goldlöckchen did after being discovered in bed by die drei Bären.

subLevels.reveal: The kiss is Disney's invention, added in the 1937 animated film. In the original Brothers Grimm story, the prince has the glass coffin carried away by his servants. One stumbles, the piece of poisoned apple is jolted from her throat, and she wakes up. Less problematic with the non-consensual kiss, but then he was gonna marry a corpse, so...

subLevels.german: Schneewittchen und der Prinz lebten glücklich bis ans Ende ihrer Tage.

hints.hint: glück ~ "luck" in English. If you have good luck, you're probably ____. Now turn it into an adverb.

subLevels.reveal: This is the traditional German fairytale formula for "happily ever after". Die böse Königin certainly didn't have a glückliches fate (Glück "happiness" ~ "luck" in English) — she had to dance in hot iron shoes until she dropped dead. And this was the wedding entertainment. Talk about Grimm. Well done on wading through all the linguistic analysis! Bet you're glücklich that's behind you!
